Title: refactor(shortcut): central keyboard-shortcut registry with key sequences

Closes #56

## What changed and why

Gitea's keyboard shortcuts were one page-wide key handler that searched the page for a `<kbd>` hint showing the pressed key and focused the box beside it. That only allowed "press a letter to focus a box": no two-key sequences, no shortcut without a box, and nothing could list the shortcuts for a help dialog. This PR replaces it with one place to add shortcuts. Nothing changes for the user and `s` and `t` work as before.

- **One call to add a shortcut:** `registerShortcut()` takes the keys, a translated description, an optional section and the action to run. `getShortcuts()` lists the shortcuts on the current page, for the help dialog in #57.
- **Two-key sequences** such as `g c`: the second key must come within 1500 ms. Pressing `g` does nothing else while it waits, and a key that doesn't finish a sequence counts as a fresh press.
- **Shortcuts stay out of the way:** nothing runs while typing in a field, while Ctrl, Alt or Cmd is held, or when a widget such as a menu has already used the key.
- **Clashes fail loudly:** adding the same keys twice, or keys where one starts the other (a lone `g` and `g c`), throws an error instead of one silently winning.
- **A shortcut can belong to part of the page,** and only exists while that part is on the page. This is what lets the `T` hint come back after moving through the file tree, which swaps the page content, without counting as a clash.
- **The `S` and `T` hints register themselves** through the new code. Each is listed with its box's placeholder ("Search code…", "Go to file") and the existing "Repository" string as its section, so no new string was needed.
- The docs in `.claude-students` are updated with additions and corrections from this implementation

## How the changes relate to the ACs

- **AC1:** `s` on a repository home page focuses the code search box and hides its hint; `t` does the same for "Go to file" on file and folder views.
- **AC2:** Escape in a box with a hint clears it and moves focus away, as before.
- **AC3:** a single-key shortcut such as `?` runs once, and the key does nothing else.
- **AC4:** `g` then `c` within 1500 ms runs the sequence once, and neither key runs a shortcut of its own.
- **AC5:** after more than 1500 ms, or after a key that doesn't finish any sequence, the `g` is dropped and the next key is a fresh press.
- **AC6:** keys typed into an input, textarea, select or editable area run no shortcut and type as normal.
- **AC7:** a key a widget has already used runs no shortcut and drops a half-typed sequence.
- **AC8:** adding the same keys again, or keys where one starts the other, throws; a hint that loads again after file-tree navigation is not an error, and its key keeps working.
- **AC9:** each listed shortcut has its keys, description and, if given, section; `s` and `t` use their box's placeholder and are in the Repository section.

## How it was tested

### Test strategy

There were no tests for keyboard shortcuts before this PR, so every test here is new.

- **Unit tests (Vitest) for the logic.** Most of the changes related to rules about which key presses run which shortcut. These need no server, so they are tested on their own with a fake clock so the timeout tests don't have to wait. The registry tests each build their own list of shortcuts, and the hint tests clear the page after each test, so no test leaks into another. 17 tests in `web_src/js/modules/shortcut.test.ts`.
- **Playwright tests for the wiring.** The `S` and `T` hints only work once Gitea's templates, the Vue "Go to file" box and the page setup code have all run, and none of that exists in a unit test. Three tests in tests/e2e/shortcut.test.ts drive real pages for what depends on that wiring: the hints (AC1, AC2, AC6, AC9), a key the language menu uses (AC7) and the file tree (AC8).

**Testing the tests.** Mutation testing performed during implementation of tests to ensure they actually catch the intended errors. Each break made the matching test fail, so the tests check the behaviour and don't just run.

**Not covered automatically, and why.** AC3, AC4 and AC5 have no real-page test, because no page has a sequence or a `?` shortcut yet; they get one when #57 and #58 add them.

**Checked by hand.** Claude also drove a headless browser through a local instance, and I had a look to ensure the changes actually did not change visible/user facing behavior.

**Misc.** Token heavy review workflow with reviewers and critics was run at the end to ensure things were not overlooked.

| AC9 | The list gives keys, description and section, and drops a shortcut whose element left the page; a hint is listed with its box's placeholder and section; the real hints carry the Repository section |

# Design Decision for the first commit (the shortcut registry)

### Decision 1: Shortcuts are kept in one list in the page code, and a shortcut can belong to a part of the page

**Decision:** Shortcuts are added to a single list in the page code, each with its keys, a description and an optional section, and one key handler serves them all. A shortcut can belong to a part of the page, such as the search box its `S` hint sits beside, and only exists while that part is on the page.
**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Keep the page's HTML as the list, as today: on each key press, look for a hint showing that key. (b) Have whatever adds a shortcut remove it again when its part of the page goes away. (c) Let the newest shortcut for a key replace the older one.
**Rationale:** (a) can't hold a shortcut that has no box to focus, like `?` or `g c`, and gives the help dialog (#57) nothing to list. (b) has nothing to hang the removal on: moving through the file tree swaps the page content without tearing down what was in it. (c) would let two shortcuts on the same key pass silently, which AC8 rules out. Tying a shortcut to its part of the page lets a hint that the file tree reloads come back without an error, and keeps the list accurate after moving around.
**Consequences:** Adding a shortcut is one call, and shortcuts with no box become possible. A part of the page that is hidden but not removed still counts as present, so #58 and #59 must tie their shortcuts to something that gets removed, or check for themselves. Finding out what a key does now means looking at the list in the code as well as the HTML.

# Design Decision for the third commit (sections for the shortcut list)

### Decision 2: Each hint names its own section in the page's HTML

**Decision:** A hint states its translated section ("Repository") on itself, beside the key it already declares. The "Go to file" box receives it the same way it already receives its placeholder text.
**Alternatives Considered:** (a) A hint takes its section from the part of the page it sits in, declared once on a surrounding element. (b) Send the section names to every page along with the few general strings Gitea already gives the page code.
**Rationale:** (a) needs fewer edits, but a hint's section would depend on markup far away from it, and moving a hint could silently change its section. (b) is reserved for general text by a comment where it is set up, and the sections for #57–#59 would pile up there. Declaring it on the hint keeps everything about a shortcut in one place, and follows how Gitea already hands translated text to page code: tooltips, confirm dialogs and the file finder's own placeholder each use an attribute named for what it holds.
**Consequences:** A new hint that forgets its section is listed without one. The "Go to file" box gains one more setting passed through to it. The existing "Repository" string is reused, so it is already translated. Shortcuts added from code give their section directly, so this only concerns hints.

XXXXX
Notes for the PR's `## Tech Debt` section. Only real items, added as they come up.

**Introduced:**
- (none yet)

**Encountered:**
- Moving through the file tree replaces `.repo-view-content` with `innerHTML` but the Vue "Go to file" app mounted inside it is never unmounted, so each navigation leaves one detached app behind. Handled by not relying on cleanup: a shortcut tied to an element that has left the page is replaced when its hint registers again. Not fixed here.
- Page setup (`data-global-init`) has no error isolation and an error in the setup of one element on page load will lead to every other element being unset. A second hint for the same key now throws there (AC8), so that clash would break the rest of the page's setup. Handled by following the existing pattern, since setup already throws on other developer mistakes such as a misspelled init name. Not fixed here.

# Issue #56 -- Central keyboard-shortcut registry with chords

## Class Diagram

![Class diagram](56-ab-wm-class.png)

**Notation.** This issue is TypeScript, Vue and Go templates rather than Go, so the diagram maps
them as follows. A TypeScript `class` is a UML class. A module (a file of functions and
module-level variables, such as `shortcut.ts`) is a class with the «module» stereotype: exported
functions are `+`, unexported ones `-`. A TypeScript `type` is a class with «type», a Vue component
is a «component» with its props as attributes, a Go template is a «template» with the attributes it
renders, and a browser custom element is a «custom element». A `data-global-init` attribute that
makes one file run another's code is drawn as a dependency. In Go code the same approach maps a
struct to a class, an interface to an «interface» that structs realize, and struct embedding to
composition.

## Sequence Diagram

![Sequence diagram](56-ab-wm-sequence.png)

## Q&A

**Class diagram:**

1. Among all the classes shown in the diagram, which 1--2 are most central to understanding the codebase and solving the issue? Explain what role each one plays.

   The `ShortcutRegistry`, which is new in this PR, holds every shortcut on a page. Its `register()` function enforces the "clash" rule, which ensures that a set of keys has only one meaning on a page. This class was necessary because, prior to this PR, there was no central place for shortcut handling or behavior, and the HTML of the page itself was the only record of what shortcuts existed. The class also has the `handleKeyDown()` function, which handles all of the key presses.

2. What is the most significant relationship shown in the diagram? Explain what it represents in the system and why it matters for understanding the solution.

   A `Shortcut` can be attached to an `HTMLElement`. This is of utmost importance, especially from the point of view of lifetimes and avoiding clashes. Thanks to this association, the registry notices on its own when the element is no longer on the page (`element.isConnected`). Of course, this led to the introduced tech debt, as "on the page" is not the same as "visible", so a shortcut keeps working, and can still clash, even when its element is hidden.

3. Looking back at your implementation, is there anything in this design you would change, and why?

   There are two changes I would have made, but both would have been "intrusive" or unnecessary for the task at hand:

   - A clashing hint fails loudly and breaks the rest of the page's setup, but avoiding that meant handling the error differently from how the rest of Gitea's setup handles mistakes, which is not ideal.
   - Hidden elements count as present, as noted in 2. The solution could be a visibility check, but that also means key presses would need layout reads, so it is a tough decision to make.

**Sequence diagram:**

1. What user action or system event starts the sequence, and what is the expected outcome when it completes successfully?

   The sequence starts when the user clicks a file in the repository's file tree. This sets up the sequence by first requesting the new content to load in (without reloading the page), and then setting up the page's functionality, which in the process registers the shortcut.

   Once the user presses the key (in this case, t), the listener picks it up and focuses the "Go to file" box.

2. Identify the 2--3 most important steps in the sequence. For each one, describe what is happening and note whether it involves existing code or new/modified code from your solution.

   - The `registerShortcut()` function, which is new in this solution, is the core of the functionality that moved shortcuts from being embedded in the HTML to being centrally managed. It registers the shortcut, along with the details of everything that is needed for the shortcut to function.
   - The other important step is `globalRegistry.handleKeyDown(e)`, which is also new in this solution. It is part of centralizing the shortcuts, where there is now just one function that tracks and handles the processing of relevant key presses. It receives the page's key presses, processes them, and when it finds one it is tracking, sets off the required changes.

3. What error cases or alternative paths are not shown in the diagram, and why did you leave them out?

   A few things were left out: the error during a clash (e.g. a second live T hint), which throws during page setup; the details of how keys are processed, such as two-key sequences and the 1500 ms timeout, since no real page uses a sequence yet and the unit tests cover them; and the first page load, which is essentially just this diagram without the replacement of elements.

**Cross-cutting:**

4. If you used AI to create or check any part of the diagrams, describe what it produced, what you verified against the actual code, and what you had to correct or add. If AI was not used, write "N/A."

   AI (Claude Code, claude-opus-5-5) produced both diagrams, including their callouts, modelled on the course's reference diagrams (hence the similar style).

   For the class diagram, I inspected the diagram to ensure that all the included elements actually make sense; commits were small on purpose, and thus, many of the classes were familiar. For anything I did not understand, I had a quick look through the commits again to see where they came from.

   The sequence diagram was a bit harder, as is the case for most of Gitea's codebase, thanks to its many interacting components. Regardless, many of the events do make sense from the commits I reviewed and the changes they implemented. I also manually traced the `handleKeyDown()` function to see how the key processing happens.

   I did not find a need to change anything after the fact, other than a few guiding notes on scope. This was likely because the AI agent that produced these diagrams also implemented the changes.

## Branches and commits

- Branches: `feat/issue-<N>-short-description`, `fix/issue-<N>-short-description` or
  `chore/short-description` (`STUDENTS.md`). One issue per branch.
- Commit messages follow Conventional Commits and end with the issue number:
  `feat(repo): show empty state on releases page (#17)`. Add an
  `Assisted-by: AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION` trailer when AI helped; never `Co-Authored-By` or
  `Signed-off-by` (`AGENTS.md`). A human approves every commit before it is made.

### Before each implementation: sync with main

Every new branch starts from an up-to-date `main`. AI sessions run this before writing any code:

```bash
git switch main
git pull origin main
git switch -c feat/issue-<N>-short-description
```

To pick up new work on `main` for a branch that already exists, **merge, don't rebase**. Rebasing
or squashing after review has started is not allowed (`docs/sprint0/standards.md`):

```bash
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main
```

Do this before opening the PR and again if `main` moves while it is in review. Never merge another
feature branch into yours.

### After merge: clean up

A PR is merged with a merge commit once it is approved, every review comment is addressed and CI
passes. Then:

```bash
git switch main
git pull origin main
git branch -d feat/issue-<N>-short-description               # local branch
git push origin --delete feat/issue-<N>-short-description    # or GitHub's "Delete branch" button
git fetch --prune                                            # drop stale remote-tracking refs
```

Also check that the issue closed (via `Closes #N`), is on the sprint milestone, and has its AI
Assistance comment. Then run `specstory sync` and file the session's log (see `ai-logs/README.md`).

Template: `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Title uses Conventional Commits, e.g.
`fix(issues): keep label filter after search`. Description sections:

1. `Closes #<N>`, which links the issue and closes it on merge.
2. **What changed:** the change in your own words.
3. **Why:** the problem, and which acceptance criteria (AC1…) it satisfies.
4. **How it was tested / Test strategy:** tests added or updated and why these ones. Name any

Posted by each contributor on the **issue** they worked, once their work is done. One comment per
person — never edit someone else's. Add later sessions by editing your own table.

## User Story

As a front-end developer, I want one place to add keyboard shortcuts, including two-key sequences like `g c`, so that I can add a shortcut and have it listed in a help dialog without editing the page-wide key handler each time.

## User Scenario
Nothing changes for the end user in this issue, as all changes attempt to refactor code while keeping the current functionality intact; pressing `s` on a repository home page still focuses the sidebar search, and `t` on the code view focuses the "Go to file" box. Only underlying code will change, where a developer adding a shortcut now calls `registerShortcut()` instead of adding another branch to the global `keydown` handler.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given the repository home page, when the user presses `s` with focus outside a text field, then the code search box is focused and its `S` hint hides; `t` does the same for the "Go to file" box on file and folder views.
- [ ] AC2: Given focus is in a box that shows a shortcut hint, when the user presses Escape, then the box is cleared and loses focus, as it does today.
- [ ] AC3: Given a single-key shortcut such as `?` is added from code, when the user presses that key with focus outside a text field, then its action runs once and the key does nothing else.
- [ ] AC4: Given the two-key sequence `g c` is added, when the user presses `g` and then `c` within 1500 ms, then its action runs once and neither key runs a single-key shortcut of its own.
- [ ] AC5: Given the same sequence, when the user presses `g` and then waits longer than 1500 ms, or presses a key that does not finish any sequence, then the `g` is dropped and the second key acts as a fresh press.
- [ ] AC6: Given focus is in an input, textarea, select or editable area, when the user presses a key that has a shortcut, then no shortcut runs and the key types as normal.
- [ ] AC7: Given a menu or other widget has already used a key (for example a menu jumping to an item when the user types its first letter), when the key reaches the page, then no shortcut runs and any half-finished sequence is dropped.
- [ ] AC8: Given a shortcut already exists for some keys, when code adds the same keys again, or keys where one is the start of the other (a lone `g` and `g c`), then adding it fails with an error; an `S` or `T` hint that loads again, for example while moving through the file tree, is not an error and its key keeps working.
- [ ] AC9: Given the shortcuts on a page, when they are listed, then each one has its keys, a short translated description and, if given, a section label; s and t use their box's placeholder text ("Search code…" and "Go to file") and are in the repository section.

## Out of Scope
- Help dialog that lists the shortcuts, and turning section labels into headings: Issue (#57)
- `g` navigation shortcuts: Issue (#58)
- `c` to focus the comment box: Issue (#59)
- Turning shortcuts off: Issue (#60)
- Shortcuts that use Ctrl, Alt or Cmd (e.g. Ctrl/Cmd+K). None of the planned shortcuts need one, so those presses keep being ignored, as they are today.
- Remapping shortcuts by the user, or saving anything to the server.
- The code editor's and Markdown editor's own keys, which stay where they are.

## Open Questions
None

## Design Decisions
Below

## Scope
medium (5 points)

## AI Disclosure
Used claude-code for the drafting of this issue, followed by my changes and proofing.

let globalSelectorObserverInited = false;

type SelectorHandler<T extends Element> = {selector: string, handler: (el: T) => void};
const selectorHandlers: SelectorHandler<Element>[] = [];

type GlobalEventFunc<T extends HTMLElement, E extends Event> = (el: T, e: E) => Promisable<void>;
const globalEventFuncs: Record<string, GlobalEventFunc<HTMLElement, Event>> = {};

type GlobalInitFunc<T extends Element> = (el: T) => Promisable<void>;
const globalInitFuncs: Record<string, GlobalInitFunc<Element>> = {};

// It handles the global events for all `<div data-global-click="onSomeElemClick"></div>` elements.
export function registerGlobalEventFunc<T extends HTMLElement, E extends Event>(event: string, name: string, func: GlobalEventFunc<T, E>) {
  globalEventFuncs[`${event}:${name}`] = func as GlobalEventFunc<HTMLElement, Event>;
}

// It handles the global init functions by a selector, for example:
// > registerGlobalSelectorObserver('.ui.dropdown:not(.custom)', (el) => { initDropdown(el, ...) });
// ATTENTION: For most cases, it's recommended to use registerGlobalInitFunc instead,
// Because this selector-based approach is less efficient and less maintainable.
// But if there are already a lot of elements on many pages, this selector-based approach is more convenient for exiting code.
export function registerGlobalSelectorFunc<T extends Element>(selector: string, handler: (el: T) => void) {
  selectorHandlers.push({selector, handler: handler as (el: Element) => void});
  // Then initAddedElementObserver will call this handler for all existing elements after all handlers are added.
  // This approach makes the init stage only need to do one "querySelectorAll".
  if (!globalSelectorObserverInited) return;
  for (const el of document.querySelectorAll<T>(selector)) {
    handler(el);
  }
}

// It handles the global init functions for all `<div data-global-int="initSomeElem"></div>` elements.
export function registerGlobalInitFunc<T extends HTMLElement>(name: string, handler: GlobalInitFunc<T>) {
  globalInitFuncs[name] = handler as GlobalInitFunc<Element>;
  // The "global init" functions are managed internally and called by callGlobalInitFunc
  // They must be ready before initGlobalSelectorObserver is called.
  if (globalSelectorObserverInited) throw new Error('registerGlobalInitFunc() must be called before initGlobalSelectorObserver()');
}

function callGlobalInitFunc(el: Element) {
  // TODO: GLOBAL-INIT-MULTIPLE-FUNCTIONS: maybe in the future we need to extend it to support multiple functions, for example: `data-global-init="func1 func2 func3"`
  const initFunc = el.getAttribute('data-global-init')!;
  const func = globalInitFuncs[initFunc];
  if (!func) throw new Error(`Global init function "${initFunc}" not found`);

  // when an element node is removed and added again, it should not be re-initialized again.
  type GiteaGlobalInitElement = Partial<Element> & {_giteaGlobalInited: boolean};
  if ((el as GiteaGlobalInitElement)._giteaGlobalInited) return;
  (el as GiteaGlobalInitElement)._giteaGlobalInited = true;

  func(el);
}

function attachGlobalEvents() {
  // add global "[data-global-click]" event handler
  document.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
    const elem = (e.target as HTMLElement).closest<HTMLElement>('[data-global-click]');
    if (!elem) return;
    const funcName = elem.getAttribute('data-global-click');
    const func = globalEventFuncs[`click:${funcName}`];
    if (!func) throw new Error(`Global event function "click:${funcName}" not found`);
    func(elem, e);
  });
}

> Sub-issue of #23 · **P1** · estimate **5 points** (medium) · blocked by #56
## User Story
As a user who suspects Gitea has keyboard shortcuts but cannot find them, I want to press `?` on
any page and see every available shortcut grouped by area, so that I can learn them without
reading the source or the docs.
## User Scenario
A user is looking at an issue. They press `?`. A dialog opens in the centre of the page titled
"Keyboard shortcuts", listing the shortcuts under headings such as "Site-wide" and "Repository",
each row showing the keys as `<kbd>` elements next to a description. Focus moves into the dialog;
Tab cycles inside it and does not reach the page behind. They press Escape, the dialog closes, and
focus returns to where it was.
## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given any page with focus on the document body, when the user presses `?`, then a
      dialog opens listing one row per shortcut registered in #56, with the keys and the
      description.
- [ ] AC2: Given the dialog is open, when the user presses Escape, then it closes and focus
      returns to the element that was focused before it opened.
- [ ] AC3: Given the dialog is open, when the user presses Tab repeatedly, then focus stays inside
      the dialog and never lands on a control on the page behind it.
- [ ] AC4: Given focus is in a comment textarea, when the user types `?`, then a literal `?` is
      inserted and the dialog does not open.
- [ ] AC5: Given a new shortcut is registered with a description and a category, when the dialog
      is opened, then it appears under that category with no change to the dialog's own code.
- [ ] AC6: Given the page is served in a non-English locale, when the dialog is opened, then the
      title and section headings are rendered from locale keys, not hard-coded English.
- [ ] AC7: A Playwright test in `tests/e2e/` covers AC1, AC2 and AC4 and passes `assertNoJsError`.
## Out of Scope
- Adding shortcuts. The dialog lists whatever #56's registry holds, which at merge time is `s`,
  `t` and `?` itself.
- Editing or remapping a shortcut from the dialog.
- The opt-out checkbox — that is #60.
- A printable or documentation-page version of the list.
## Open Questions
- Should the dialog also be reachable by mouse, from a footer link? Proposed: not in this issue,
  to keep it to one entry point that the e2e test can cover.
## Design Decision
**Decision:** Build the dialog on the native `<dialog>` element with `showModal()`, not on
Fomantic's modal.
**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Fomantic modal via `showFomanticModal` in
`web_src/js/modules/fomantic/modal.ts`, which is what the rest of the codebase uses today.
(b) A plain `<div>` with a hand-written focus trap and backdrop.
**Rationale:** `.claude-students/docs/frontend-js.md` says Fomantic is deprecated and new features
must not be built on it — and given this issue's sibling #25 exists to remove Fomantic for
accessibility reasons, adding a new Fomantic modal to the accessibility feature would be
(eval):1: ===== not found

<!-- markdownlint-disable MD029 -->
<!-- Rules are numbered continuously 1-15 across the sections below; check.sh error
     messages and all 34 docs cite them by number, so the sequence must not restart. -->

# Maintenance rules

Five people maintain one shared set of docs. These rules exist so the set stays *one* set. Read
them before editing anything in `.claude-students/`. Rules marked **[checked]** are enforced by
`./.claude-students/check.sh`.

## Scope discipline

1. **Upstream wins.** `AGENTS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `docs/guidelines-*.md` are authoritative.
   Docs here summarise them and link to them; they never restate a rule differently and never
   contradict one. A contradiction is a bug in this folder, not in the project.
2. **One fact, one home.** Every fact lives in exactly one doc — the one whose `scope:` owns that
   path. Everywhere else, link to it. Duplicated facts are how five maintainers end up with five
   different answers.
3. **Durability test.** Record a fact only if it (a) took more than one discovery step to find and
   (b) will still be true after the next upstream merge. A one-off workaround, a sprint detail or
   anything about your own task fails this test — that belongs in `ai-logs/`.
4. **No process notes.** No TODOs, no open questions, no first person, no student names, no dates
   other than `verified-at`. This is a map of the code, not a journal.

## Form

5. **Template only [checked].** Use the `## ` headings from `_TEMPLATE.md`, all of them, in that
   order, with nothing added. If a section has nothing to say, write one line saying so.
6. **120-line cap [checked].** Going over means the scope is too broad. Split the doc, and add the
   new `INDEX.md` row in the same commit. `INDEX.md` itself is capped at 60 lines.
7. **Cite or delete [checked, partially].** Every claim names a repo path. A claim with no path is
   unverifiable by the next reader — delete it.
8. **Symbols, not line numbers [checked].** Write `models/db/context.go` → `WithTx`, never
   `models/db/context.go:143`. Line numbers rot at the next upstream merge and a stale number is
   worse than no number. Code fences stay at 10 lines or fewer — point at the file instead of
   copying it.
9. **Repo-relative paths [checked].** `models/db/context.go`, never `/home/you/gitea/models/...`.
10. **Whitespace [checked].** No trailing whitespace, LF endings, final newline — same as the rest
    of the repo (`.editorconfig`).

## Change control

11. **One universal set.** These docs live on `main` and nowhere else. Never keep a personal copy,
    a per-student folder, or a long-lived branch of them.
12. **Changes land by PR**, titled `docs(context): <subject>` per `AGENTS.md` Conventional Commits,
    with an `Assisted-by: AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION` trailer and no `Co-Authored-By` or
    `Signed-off-by`.
13. **Fix in place.** If you discover while working that a doc is wrong or incomplete, correct it
    in the *same* PR as your code change and update `verified-at` to the commit you checked
    against. Leaving a doc stale for someone else to hit is the exact failure this folder exists to
    prevent. This rule applies to AI sessions too.
14. **New docs need three things in one commit [checked]:** the file, its `INDEX.md` row, and a
    `scope:` that does not overlap any existing doc's. If the scope overlaps, you wanted to edit
    that doc, not add one.
15. **`./.claude-students/check.sh` passes before you push [checked].** It is dependency-free and
    finishes in under a second.

## The guide layer (rules 16-22)

`guide/` holds a plain-English page for each reference page in `docs/`, same filename. It exists so
a person new to Go and to this codebase can get oriented. It is **derived**, not independent.

16. Every guide carries `source:`, `source-hash:` and `verified-at:` in its frontmatter **[checked]**.
17. A guide's `source:` names a real `docs/*.md` with the **same filename** **[checked]**.
18. `source-hash:` is the first 16 characters of `sha256sum docs/<name>.md`. If the reference page
    changes and the guide is not regenerated, `check.sh` reports **drift** **[checked]**. Regenerating
    means: reread the reference page, rewrite the guide, update the hash and `verified-at`.
19. Guide headings match `guide/_TEMPLATE.md` exactly and in order **[checked]**.
20. Guides are capped at **200 lines**, code fences at **30** **[checked]** — teaching needs more room
    than reference does.
21. **A guide adds explanation, vocabulary and worked steps. It adds no new facts.** Every repo path
    a guide cites must also be cited by its source page **[checked]**. If you need a fact the
    reference page lacks, add it *there* first, which bumps the hash and forces the guide to be
    regenerated in the same commit — exactly the intended order.
22. `guide/START-HERE.md` has no source page. It is exempt from rules 17, 18 and 21, and is where
    cross-cutting material lives that no single reference page owns.

**Never fix a fact in `guide/`.** If the two layers disagree, the reference page is the truth and
the guide is stale: fix `docs/`, regenerate the guide, ship both in one PR. A disagreement is a bug
report against `docs/`, not an editing job in `guide/`.

> Sub-issue of #23 · **P3 — Sprint 2 carryover** · estimate **2 points** (small) · blocked by #56, #57

## User Story
As a user of speech recognition software, I want to turn off Gitea's single-character shortcuts,
so that dictating a word into the page does not fire a shortcut and navigate me away from what I
was writing.

## User Scenario
Someone using voice control finds that saying a word while the page has focus keeps triggering the
file finder. They press `?`, see a checkbox at the bottom of the shortcut dialog reading "Enable
character key shortcuts", and clear it. The shortcut list greys out. They close the dialog, dictate
freely, and the setting is still off the next time they open Gitea in that browser.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given the shortcut help dialog, when the user clears the "Enable character key
      shortcuts" checkbox, then pressing `s`, `t` or any `g` sequence has no effect.
- [ ] AC2: Given shortcuts are disabled, when the user reloads the page, then they are still
      disabled.
- [ ] AC3: Given shortcuts are disabled, when the user presses `?`, then the help dialog still
      opens, so the setting can be turned back on without a mouse.
- [ ] AC4: Given shortcuts are disabled, when the user re-checks the box, then `s` focuses the
      repo sidebar search again without a reload.
- [ ] AC5: Given a browser with storage blocked, when the page loads, then shortcuts default to
      enabled and no error is thrown.
- [ ] AC6: Unit tests in `web_src/js/modules/shortcut.test.ts` cover AC1, AC3 and AC5.

## Out of Scope
- Remapping individual shortcuts, or turning off one shortcut at a time.
- Storing the preference on the server or syncing it across devices or browsers.
- A copy of the toggle in the user settings pages.

## Open Questions
- WCAG 2.1 SC 2.1.4 is satisfied by "turn off", "remap" or "active on focus only". This issue
  takes "turn off" as the cheapest complete option; confirm that is the team's reading.

## Design Decision
**Decision:** Store the preference in `localStorage` and keep `?` itself exempt from the toggle.

**Alternatives Considered:** (a) A server-side user setting, as a column on the user table with a
checkbox on the appearance settings page. (b) Storing it in `localStorage` but suppressing every
shortcut including `?`.

**Rationale:** (a) needs a migration and a settings form for a preference that is per-browser by
nature — someone using voice control on one machine does not need it off everywhere — and a
migration is more than this issue is worth. (b) is more literally correct against SC 2.1.4, but it
leaves a keyboard-only user who has disabled shortcuts with no keyboard route back to the dialog,
which trades one accessibility failure for another; keeping exactly one exempt key is the standard
escape hatch.

**Consequences:** Easier — no server change, no migration, and the flag is a single module-level
read the registry consults before dispatching. Harder — the preference does not follow the user to
another browser or machine and is invisible to support; and `?` staying live is a documented
deliberate exception that needs a comment in the code so nobody "fixes" it later.

# Design Decision for the first commit (the shortcut registry)

### Decision 1: Shortcuts are kept in one list in the page code, and a shortcut can belong to a part of the page

**Decision:** Shortcuts are added to a single list in the page code, each with its keys, a description and an optional section, and one key handler serves them all. A shortcut can belong to a part of the page, such as the search box its `S` hint sits beside, and only exists while that part is on the page.
**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Keep the page's HTML as the list, as today: on each key press, look for a hint showing that key. (b) Have whatever adds a shortcut remove it again when its part of the page goes away. (c) Let the newest shortcut for a key replace the older one.
**Rationale:** (a) can't hold a shortcut that has no box to focus, like `?` or `g c`, and gives the help dialog (#57) nothing to list. (b) has nothing to hang the removal on: moving through the file tree swaps the page content without tearing down what was in it. (c) would let two shortcuts on the same key pass silently, which AC8 rules out. Tying a shortcut to its part of the page lets a hint that the file tree reloads come back without an error, and keeps the list accurate after moving around.
**Consequences:** Adding a shortcut is one call, and shortcuts with no box become possible. A part of the page that is hidden but not removed still counts as present, so #58 and #59 must tie their shortcuts to something that gets removed, or check for themselves. Finding out what a key does now means looking at the list in the code as well as the HTML.

# Design Decision for the third commit (sections for the shortcut list)

### Decision 2: Each hint names its own section in the page's HTML

**Decision:** A hint states its translated section ("Repository") on itself, beside the key it already declares. The "Go to file" box receives it the same way it already receives its placeholder text.
**Alternatives Considered:** (a) A hint takes its section from the part of the page it sits in, declared once on a surrounding element. (b) Send the section names to every page along with the few general strings Gitea already gives the page code.
**Rationale:** (a) needs fewer edits, but a hint's section would depend on markup far away from it, and moving a hint could silently change its section. (b) is reserved for general text by a comment where it is set up, and the sections for #57–#59 would pile up there. Declaring it on the hint keeps everything about a shortcut in one place, and follows how Gitea already hands translated text to page code: tooltips, confirm dialogs and the file finder's own placeholder each use an attribute named for what it holds.
**Consequences:** A new hint that forgets its section is listed without one. The "Go to file" box gains one more setting passed through to it. The existing "Repository" string is reused, so it is already translated. Shortcuts added from code give their section directly, so this only concerns hints.

## Branches and commits

- Branches: `feat/issue-<N>-short-description`, `fix/issue-<N>-short-description` or
  `chore/short-description` (`STUDENTS.md`). One issue per branch.
- Commit messages follow Conventional Commits and end with the issue number:
  `feat(repo): show empty state on releases page (#17)`. Add an
  `Assisted-by: AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION` trailer when AI helped; never `Co-Authored-By` or
  `Signed-off-by` (`AGENTS.md`). A human approves every commit before it is made.

### Before each implementation: sync with main

Every new branch starts from an up-to-date `main`. AI sessions run this before writing any code:

```bash
git switch main
git pull origin main
git switch -c feat/issue-<N>-short-description
```

To pick up new work on `main` for a branch that already exists, **merge, don't rebase**. Rebasing
or squashing after review has started is not allowed (`docs/sprint0/standards.md`):

```bash
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main
```

Do this before opening the PR and again if `main` moves while it is in review. Never merge another
feature branch into yours.

### After merge: clean up

A PR is merged with a merge commit once it is approved, every review comment is addressed and CI
passes. Then:

```bash
git switch main
git pull origin main
git branch -d feat/issue-<N>-short-description               # local branch
git push origin --delete feat/issue-<N>-short-description    # or GitHub's "Delete branch" button
git fetch --prune                                            # drop stale remote-tracking refs
```

Also check that the issue closed (via `Closes #N`), is on the sprint milestone, and has its AI
Assistance comment. Then run `specstory sync` and file the session's log (see `ai-logs/README.md`).

## Issue format: feature (user story)

Template: `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/user-story.yaml`. The user story must meet INVEST: Independent,
Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.

```markdown
## User Story
As a <role>, I want <capability> so that <benefit>.

## User Scenario
<A short concrete walk-through: who, where in the UI, what they do, what they see.>

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given <state>, when <action>, then <observable result>.
- [ ] AC2: ...
- [ ] AC3: ...            (at least 3; each has a clear pass/fail result)

## Out of Scope
- <What this issue deliberately does not do.>

## Open Questions
- <Unresolved questions, or "None".>

## Design Decision
**Decision:** <what was chosen>
**Alternatives Considered:** <at least two concrete options, and why each lost>
**Rationale:** <why this one>
**Consequences:** <trade-offs, follow-up work, what it makes harder>

## Scope
small | medium | large, and matching `scope:` label
```

## Issue format: bug report

Template: `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug-report.yaml`.

```markdown
## Observed Behavior
## Expected Behavior
## Steps to Reproduce
1. ...
## Additional Information
<Version or commit, browser/OS, logs, screenshots.>
## Design Decision
<Same four fields as above: Decision, Alternatives Considered, Rationale, Consequences.>
```

- **Design Decision (D3):** fill it in once you've picked an approach, before opening the PR. Put
  a second decision under another `### Decision 2` heading. If a PR changes the decision, update
  the issue body.
- **Peer review (D2):** a teammate reads the spec and comments `Spec reviewed — <notes>` on the
  issue before implementation starts.

## Pull request format

Template: `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Title uses Conventional Commits, e.g.
`fix(issues): keep label filter after search`. Description sections:

1. `Closes #<N>`, which links the issue and closes it on merge.
2. **What changed:** the change in your own words.
3. **Why:** the problem, and which acceptance criteria (AC1…) it satisfies.
4. **How it was tested / Test strategy:** tests added or updated and why these ones. Name any
   change that can't be tested automatically and how it was checked by hand. Every behaviour change
   needs a new or updated test.
5. **CI / manual verification:** CI status, or the commands run and their results.
6. **Design:** one line pointing at the Design Decision in the issue, or a note on how it changed.
7. **Tech Debt:** required from Sprint 2. Both fields are required, and `None.` is a valid answer:

   ```markdown
   ## Tech Debt

   **Introduced:** <shortcuts, workarounds or design compromises this PR makes, and why>

   **Encountered:** <tech debt that was already there and that you ran into, and how you handled it>
   ```

8. **AI assistance:** format in `AI-ASSISTANCE.md` §2, with **no log link**.

Per-PR grading (20 points): correctness against the acceptance criteria 6, test strategy with
explanation 5, description quality including the Tech Debt section 4, CI or manual verification 3,
review rubric posted 2.

## Code review rubric

The reviewer posts this as a **PR comment**, as well as the GitHub review itself. A copy-paste copy
is in `.github/code-review-rubric.md`, so keep the two in sync. Pull the branch and test it when you
can, say what you checked, and mark each point as required or optional
(`docs/community-governance.md`). Score each row against the issue's acceptance criteria. Anything
below 7 needs a note saying what would raise it.

```markdown
### Code Review — @reviewer-username

**Checked:** <what you ran or tried>

| Criterion | Score (1–10) | Notes |

| Correctness — implements issue requirements | | |
| Test coverage — tests present and meaningful | | |
| Code quality — style, naming, no duplication | | |
| Documentation — comments and PR description clear | | |
| AI transparency — evidence of human verification if AI used | | |
| Overall — merge as-is? | | |
```

--- .specstory/issue-56-pr-description.md
Title: refactor(shortcut): central keyboard-shortcut registry with key sequences

Closes #56

## What changed and why

Gitea's keyboard shortcuts were one page-wide key handler that searched the page for a `<kbd>` hint showing the pressed key and focused the box beside it. That only allowed "press a letter to focus a box": no two-key sequences, no shortcut without a box, and nothing could list the shortcuts for a help dialog. This PR replaces it with one place to add shortcuts. Nothing changes for the user and `s` and `t` work as before.

- **One call to add a shortcut:** `registerShortcut()` takes the keys, a translated description, an optional section and the action to run. `getShortcuts()` lists the shortcuts on the current page, for the help dialog in #57.
- **Two-key sequences** such as `g c`: the second key must come within 1500 ms. Pressing `g` does nothing else while it waits, and a key that doesn't finish a sequence counts as a fresh press.
- **Shortcuts stay out of the way:** nothing runs while typing in a field, while Ctrl, Alt or Cmd is held, or when a widget such as a menu has already used the key.
- **Clashes fail loudly:** adding the same keys twice, or keys where one starts the other (a lone `g` and `g c`), throws an error instead of one silently winning.
- **A shortcut can belong to part of the page,** and only exists while that part is on the page. This is what lets the `T` hint come back after moving through the file tree, which swaps the page content, without counting as a clash.
- **The `S` and `T` hints register themselves** through the new code. Each is listed with its box's placeholder ("Search code…", "Go to file") and the existing "Repository" string as its section, so no new string was needed.
- The docs in `.claude-students` are updated with additions and corrections from this implementation

## How the changes relate to the ACs

- **AC1:** `s` on a repository home page focuses the code search box and hides its hint; `t` does the same for "Go to file" on file and folder views.
- **AC2:** Escape in a box with a hint clears it and moves focus away, as before.
- **AC3:** a single-key shortcut such as `?` runs once, and the key does nothing else.
- **AC4:** `g` then `c` within 1500 ms runs the sequence once, and neither key runs a shortcut of its own.
- **AC5:** after more than 1500 ms, or after a key that doesn't finish any sequence, the `g` is dropped and the next key is a fresh press.
- **AC6:** keys typed into an input, textarea, select or editable area run no shortcut and type as normal.
- **AC7:** a key a widget has already used runs no shortcut and drops a half-typed sequence.
- **AC8:** adding the same keys again, or keys where one starts the other, throws; a hint that loads again after file-tree navigation is not an error, and its key keeps working.
- **AC9:** each listed shortcut has its keys, description and, if given, section; `s` and `t` use their box's placeholder and are in the Repository section.

## How it was tested

### Test strategy

There were no tests for keyboard shortcuts before this PR, so every test here is new.

- **Unit tests (Vitest) for the logic.** Most of the changes related to rules about which key presses run which shortcut. These need no server, so they are tested on their own with a fake clock so the timeout tests don't have to wait. The registry tests each build their own list of shortcuts, and the hint tests clear the page after each test, so no test leaks into another. 17 tests in `web_src/js/modules/shortcut.test.ts`.
- **Playwright tests for the wiring.** The `S` and `T` hints only work once Gitea's templates, the Vue "Go to file" box and the page setup code have all run, and none of that exists in a unit test. Three tests in tests/e2e/shortcut.test.ts drive real pages for what depends on that wiring: the hints (AC1, AC2, AC6, AC9), a key the language menu uses (AC7) and the file tree (AC8).

**Testing the tests.** Mutation testing performed during implementation of tests to ensure they actually catch the intended errors. Each break made the matching test fail, so the tests check the behaviour and don't just run.

**Not covered automatically, and why.** AC3, AC4 and AC5 have no real-page test, because no page has a sequence or a `?` shortcut yet; they get one when #57 and #58 add them.

**Checked by hand.** Claude also drove a headless browser through a local instance, and I had a look to ensure the changes actually did not change visible/user facing behavior.

**Misc.** Token heavy review workflow with reviewers and critics was run at the end to ensure things were not overlooked.

| AC | What the tests check |
| --- | --- |
| AC1 | Pressing `s` and `t` focuses each box and hides its hint, in the unit tests and on a real repository page |
| AC2 | Escape clears the box, moves focus away and brings the hint back, in both |
| AC3 | A single key runs its action once and is used up; an unregistered key is left alone; case doesn't matter and Shift alone isn't a press |
| AC4 | `g c` within 1500 ms runs once, and a single-key `c` doesn't run |
| AC5 | Waiting past 1500 ms, or pressing a key that finishes no sequence, drops the `g` and treats the key as a fresh press |
| AC6 | Input, textarea, select and editable areas run nothing; typing into a field drops a half-typed sequence; on a real page, typing `st` in the search box just types |
| AC7 | A key a widget already used runs nothing and drops a half-typed sequence; Ctrl, Alt and Cmd presses run nothing; on a real page, `s` in the language menu jumps to a language and the search box stays unfocused |
| AC8 | Duplicate and overlapping keys throw; a shortcut whose element left the page gives way to a new one; on a real page, `t` still works after moving through the file tree twice |
| AC9 | The list gives keys, description and section, and drops a shortcut whose element left the page; a hint is listed with its box's placeholder and section; the real hints carry the Repository section |

## CI / manual verification

- CI automatically runs; PR can only be merged on pass
- `make test-frontend`: 354 tests pass, including the 17 new ones.
- `make lint-js`, `make lint-templates` and `make lint-editorconfig` pass.
- The 3 Playwright tests pass locally on Chromium and Firefox.

## Design

Design decisions noted under issue #56.

## Tech Debt

**Introduced:** A shortcut tied to an element counts as present while the element is on the page, even when it is hidden. That is enough for the `S` and `T` hints, but #58 and #59, whose shortcuts should only work while their tab or button is shown, will have to tie them to something that is removed or check visibility themselves. In other words, any shortcuts need to tie themselves to an element with the same lifetime, so they stop working when it goes and can register again without a clash.

**Encountered:**
- Moving through the file tree swaps the page content but never unmounts the Vue "Go to file" box inside it, so each move leaves one detached copy behind. Handled by not relying on cleanup: a shortcut tied to an element that has left the page is replaced when its hint registers again. Not fixed here.
- Gitea's page setup (`data-global-init`) has no error isolation: if one element's setup throws while the page loads, every element after it is left unset. A second hint for the same key now throws there (AC8), so that mistake would break the rest of the page's setup. This follows the existing pattern, as setup already throws on other developer mistakes such as a misspelled function name. Not fixed here.

## AI assistance

Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5) drafted the code, tests, docs and other changes, ran the headless-browser checks and an automated review. I made the decisions, refused to let Claude commit on my behalf, and made commits as small as possible so I could review each one with its tests. AI-Log reference under related Issue #56

# Issue #56 -- Central keyboard-shortcut registry with chords

## Class Diagram

![Class diagram](56-ab-wm-class.png)

**Notation.** This issue is TypeScript, Vue and Go templates rather than Go, so the diagram maps
them as follows. A TypeScript `class` is a UML class. A module (a file of functions and
module-level variables, such as `shortcut.ts`) is a class with the «module» stereotype: exported
functions are `+`, unexported ones `-`. A TypeScript `type` is a class with «type», a Vue component
is a «component» with its props as attributes, a Go template is a «template» with the attributes it
renders, and a browser custom element is a «custom element». A `data-global-init` attribute that
makes one file run another's code is drawn as a dependency. In Go code the same approach maps a
struct to a class, an interface to an «interface» that structs realize, and struct embedding to
composition.

## Sequence Diagram

![Sequence diagram](56-ab-wm-sequence.png)

## Q&A

**Class diagram:**

1. Among all the classes shown in the diagram, which 1--2 are most central to understanding the codebase and solving the issue? Explain what role each one plays.

   The `ShortcutRegistry`, which is new in this PR, holds every shortcut on a page. Its `register()` function enforces the "clash" rule, which ensures that a set of keys has only one meaning on a page. This class was necessary because, prior to this PR, there was no central place for shortcut handling or behavior, and the HTML of the page itself was the only record of what shortcuts existed. The class also has the `handleKeyDown()` function, which handles all of the key presses.

2. What is the most significant relationship shown in the diagram? Explain what it represents in the system and why it matters for understanding the solution.

   A `Shortcut` can be attached to an `HTMLElement`. This is of utmost importance, especially from the point of view of lifetimes and avoiding clashes. Thanks to this association, the registry notices on its own when the element is no longer on the page (`element.isConnected`). Of course, this led to the introduced tech debt, as "on the page" is not the same as "visible", so a shortcut keeps working, and can still clash, even when its element is hidden.

3. Looking back at your implementation, is there anything in this design you would change, and why?

   There are two changes I would have made, but both would have been "intrusive" or unnecessary for the task at hand:

   - A clashing hint fails loudly and breaks the rest of the page's setup, but avoiding that meant handling the error differently from how the rest of Gitea's setup handles mistakes, which is not ideal.
   - Hidden elements count as present, as noted in 2. The solution could be a visibility check, but that also means key presses would need layout reads, so it is a tough decision to make.

**Sequence diagram:**

1. What user action or system event starts the sequence, and what is the expected outcome when it completes successfully?

   The sequence starts when the user clicks a file in the repository's file tree. This sets up the sequence by first requesting the new content to load in (without reloading the page), and then setting up the page's functionality, which in the process registers the shortcut.

   Once the user presses the key (in this case, t), the listener picks it up and focuses the "Go to file" box.

2. Identify the 2--3 most important steps in the sequence. For each one, describe what is happening and note whether it involves existing code or new/modified code from your solution.

   - The `registerShortcut()` function, which is new in this solution, is the core of the functionality that moved shortcuts from being embedded in the HTML to being centrally managed. It registers the shortcut, along with the details of everything that is needed for the shortcut to function.
   - The other important step is `globalRegistry.handleKeyDown(e)`, which is also new in this solution. It is part of centralizing the shortcuts, where there is now just one function that tracks and handles the processing of relevant key presses. It receives the page's key presses, processes them, and when it finds one it is tracking, sets off the required changes.

3. What error cases or alternative paths are not shown in the diagram, and why did you leave them out?

   A few things were left out: the error during a clash (e.g. a second live T hint), which throws during page setup; the details of how keys are processed, such as two-key sequences and the 1500 ms timeout, since no real page uses a sequence yet and the unit tests cover them; and the first page load, which is essentially just this diagram without the replacement of elements.

**Cross-cutting:**

4. If you used AI to create or check any part of the diagrams, describe what it produced, what you verified against the actual code, and what you had to correct or add. If AI was not used, write "N/A."

   AI (Claude Code, claude-opus-5-5) produced both diagrams, including their callouts, modelled on the course's reference diagrams (hence the similar style).

   For the class diagram, I inspected the diagram to ensure that all the included elements actually make sense; commits were small on purpose, and thus, many of the classes were familiar. For anything I did not understand, I had a quick look through the commits again to see where they came from.

   The sequence diagram was a bit harder, as is the case for most of Gitea's codebase, thanks to its many interacting components. Regardless, many of the events do make sense from the commits I reviewed and the changes they implemented. I also manually traced the `handleKeyDown()` function to see how the key processing happens.

   I did not find a need to change anything after the fact, other than a few guiding notes on scope. This was likely because the AI agent that produced these diagrams also implemented the changes.

56-ab-wm-sequence.png

import {env} from 'node:process';
import {test, expect} from '@playwright/test';
import type {Page} from '@playwright/test';
import {apiCreateFile, apiCreateRepo, assertNoJsError, randomString} from './utils.ts';

async function createRepo(page: Page) {
  const repoName = `e2e-shortcut-${randomString(8)}`;
  await apiCreateRepo(page.request, {name: repoName});
  await apiCreateFile(page.request, env.GITEA_TEST_E2E_USER, repoName, 'other.txt', 'other file');
  return `/${env.GITEA_TEST_E2E_USER}/${repoName}`;
}

test('s and t focus their boxes, and Escape clears them', async ({page}) => {
  await page.goto(await createRepo(page));
  const search = page.locator('.repo-home-sidebar-top input[name="q"]');
  const searchHint = page.locator('.repo-home-sidebar-top kbd');
  const goToFile = page.locator('.repo-file-search-container input');
  const goToFileHint = page.locator('.repo-file-search-container kbd');
  await expect(goToFileHint).toHaveAttribute('aria-keyshortcuts', 't'); // the Vue box has mounted and registered
  await expect(searchHint).toHaveAttribute('data-shortcut-section', 'Repository');
  await expect(goToFileHint).toHaveAttribute('data-shortcut-section', 'Repository');

  await page.keyboard.press('s');
  await expect(search).toBeFocused();
  await expect(searchHint).toBeHidden();
  await page.keyboard.type('st');
  await expect(search).toHaveValue('st');
  await page.keyboard.press('Escape');
  await expect(search).toHaveValue('');
  await expect(search).not.toBeFocused();
  await expect(searchHint).toBeVisible();

  await page.keyboard.press('t');
  await expect(goToFile).toBeFocused();
  await expect(goToFileHint).toBeHidden();
  await assertNoJsError(page);
});

test('a key the language menu uses for type-ahead runs no shortcut', async ({page}) => {
  await page.goto(await createRepo(page));
  await page.locator('aria-menu:has(.language-menu) > button').focus();
  await page.keyboard.press('Enter');
  await page.keyboard.press('s'); // jumps to a language starting with "s", such as Suomi
  await expect(page.locator('.language-menu .item:focus')).toHaveText(/^s/i);
  await expect(page.locator('.repo-home-sidebar-top input[name="q"]')).not.toBeFocused();
  await assertNoJsError(page);
});

test('t keeps working after moving through the file tree', async ({page}) => {
  const repoLink = await createRepo(page);
  await page.goto(`${repoLink}/src/branch/main/README.md`); // the file tree is shown by default
  const goToFile = page.locator('.repo-file-search-container input');
  const goToFileHint = page.locator('.repo-file-search-container kbd');

  for (const [file, content] of [['other.txt', 'other file'], ['README.md', 'e2e-shortcut-']]) {
    await page.locator(`#view-file-tree .tree-item[title="${file}"]`).click();
    await expect(page.locator('.file-view')).toContainText(content); // the page content was swapped
    await expect(goToFileHint).toHaveAttribute('aria-keyshortcuts', 't'); // the new hint has registered
    await page.keyboard.press('t');
    await expect(goToFile).toBeFocused();
    await page.keyboard.press('Escape');
  }
  await assertNoJsError(page);
});

export async function initRepoViewFileTree() {

  const repoViewContent = document.querySelector('.repo-view-content');
  if (!sidebar || !repoViewContent) return;

  registerGlobalEventFunc('click', 'onRepoViewFileTreeToggle', toggleSidebar);

  const fileTree = sidebar.querySelector('#view-file-tree')!;
  createApp(ViewFileTree, {
    repoLink: fileTree.getAttribute('data-repo-link'),
    treePath: fileTree.getAttribute('data-tree-path'),
    currentRefNameSubURL: fileTree.getAttribute('data-current-ref-name-sub-url'),
  }).mount(fileTree);

import {generateElemId, hideElem, showElem} from '../utils/dom.ts';

// A menu button following https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/menu-button/ with no Fomantic.
// Markup: <aria-menu><button type="button">label</button><div class="menu"><a class="item">...</a></div></aria-menu>
// Optional host attributes, read only by CSS: placement="bottom-start|bottom-end|top-start|top-end" (default bottom-start), pointing
// Items get real focus (roving tabindex) instead of aria-activedescendant, see web_src/js/modules/fomantic/aria.md
window.customElements.define('aria-menu', class extends HTMLElement {
  trigger!: HTMLElement;
  popup!: HTMLElement;
  inited = false;

  connectedCallback() {
    // in <head>-loaded components, the children are not parsed yet while the page is still loading
    if (document.readyState === 'loading') {
      document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', this.init, {once: true});
    } else {
      this.init();
    }
  }

  disconnectedCallback() {
    document.removeEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', this.init);
    if (this.inited) this.close(false); // also removes the outside click listener
  }

  init = () => {
    if (this.inited) return;
    const popup = this.querySelector<HTMLElement>(':scope > .menu');
    const trigger = Array.from(this.children).find((el) => el !== popup) as HTMLElement | undefined;
    if (!popup || !trigger) return;
    this.inited = true;
    this.popup = popup;
    this.trigger = trigger;

    if (trigger.tagName !== 'BUTTON') {
      trigger.setAttribute('role', 'button');
      trigger.tabIndex = 0;
    }
    if (!popup.id) popup.id = generateElemId('aria-menu-popup-');
    trigger.setAttribute('aria-haspopup', 'menu');
    trigger.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
    trigger.setAttribute('aria-controls', popup.id);
    popup.setAttribute('role', 'menu');
    if (!popup.hasAttribute('aria-label') && !popup.hasAttribute('aria-labelledby')) {
      if (!trigger.id) trigger.id = generateElemId('aria-menu-trigger-');
      popup.setAttribute('aria-labelledby', trigger.id); // keeps the menu's name once focus is on an item
    }
    hideElem(popup);
    this.updateItemRoles();

    trigger.addEventListener('click', () => this.isOpen() ? this.close(true) : this.open('first'));
    trigger.addEventListener('keydown', this.onTriggerKeyDown);
    trigger.addEventListener('keyup', this.preventSpaceClick);
    popup.addEventListener('keydown', this.onPopupKeyDown);
    popup.addEventListener('keyup', this.preventSpaceClick);
    popup.addEventListener('click', (e) => {
      // bubble phase, so the item's own click handlers have already run
      if ((e.target as Element).closest('[role="menuitem"]')) this.close(true);
    });
  };

  // items may be added after init, e.g. by a feature script, so refresh them on every open
  updateItemRoles() {
    for (const child of this.popup.children) {
      if (child.classList.contains('item')) {
        child.setAttribute('role', 'menuitem');
        child.setAttribute('tabindex', '-1');
      } else if (child.classList.contains('divider')) {
        child.setAttribute('role', 'separator');
      } else {
        child.setAttribute('role', 'none');
      }
    }
  }

  items(): HTMLElement[] {
    // hidden items can't take focus, so leaving them in would stall opening and arrow keys
    return Array.from(this.popup.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>(':scope > [role="menuitem"]:not(.tw-hidden)'));
  }

  isOpen() {
    return this.trigger.getAttribute('aria-expanded') === 'true';
  }

  open(focus: 'first' | 'last') {
    this.updateItemRoles();
    showElem(this.popup);
    this.trigger.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true');
    document.addEventListener('pointerdown', this.onPointerDownOutside, {capture: true});
    const items = this.items();
    (focus === 'first' ? items[0] : items.at(-1))?.focus();
  }

  close(restoreFocus: boolean) {
    // only restore when focus is still in the popup, so focus moved elsewhere by an item handler is kept
    const focusInPopup = this.popup.contains(document.activeElement);
    hideElem(this.popup);
    this.trigger.setAttribute('aria-expanded', 'false');
    document.removeEventListener('pointerdown', this.onPointerDownOutside, {capture: true});
    if (restoreFocus && focusInPopup) this.trigger.focus();
  }

  onPointerDownOutside = (e: Event) => {
    if (!this.contains(e.target as Node)) this.close(false);
  };

  // a native button fires "click" on Space keyup, which would toggle the menu shut again or double-activate an item
  preventSpaceClick = (e: KeyboardEvent) => {
    if (e.key === ' ') e.preventDefault();
  };

  onTriggerKeyDown = (e: KeyboardEvent) => {
    if (e.isComposing) return;
    if (e.key === 'Enter' || e.key === ' ' || e.key === 'ArrowDown') {
      this.open('first');
    } else if (e.key === 'ArrowUp') {
      this.open('last');
    } else {
      return;
    }
    e.preventDefault();
  };

  onPopupKeyDown = (e: KeyboardEvent) => {
    if (e.isComposing) return;
    const items = this.items();
    const current = items.indexOf(e.target as HTMLElement);
    if (e.key === 'Tab') {
      // focus the trigger and let the default action move on from there
      this.close(true);
      return;
    }
    if (e.key === 'Escape') {
      e.stopPropagation(); // don't also close a surrounding modal
      this.close(true);
    } else if (e.key === 'ArrowDown') {
      items[(current + 1) % items.length].focus();
    } else if (e.key === 'ArrowUp') {
      items.at(current <= 0 ? -1 : current - 1)!.focus();
    } else if (e.key === 'Home') {
      items[0].focus();
    } else if (e.key === 'End') {
      items.at(-1)!.focus();
    } else if (e.key === 'Enter' || e.key === ' ') {
      if (current < 0) return;
      items[current].click();
    } else if (e.key.length === 1 && !e.ctrlKey && !e.metaKey && !e.altKey) {
      this.focusByFirstChar(items, current, e.key);
    } else {
      return;

import {hideElem, toggleElem} from '../utils/dom.ts';

function initShortcutKbd(kbd: HTMLElement) {
  // Handle initial state: hide the kbd hint if the associated input already has a value
  // (e.g., from browser autofill or back/forward navigation cache)
  const elem = elemFromKbd(kbd);
  if (elem?.value) hideElem(kbd);
  kbd.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'true');
  kbd.setAttribute('aria-keyshortcuts', kbd.getAttribute('data-shortcut-keys')!);
}

function shortcutWrapper(el: HTMLElement): HTMLElement | null {
  const parent = el.parentElement;
  return parent?.matches('.global-shortcut-wrapper') ? parent : null;
}

function elemFromKbd(kbd: HTMLElement): HTMLInputElement | HTMLTextAreaElement | null {
  return shortcutWrapper(kbd)?.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>('input, textarea') || null;
}

function kbdFromElem(input: HTMLElement): HTMLElement | null {
  return shortcutWrapper(input)?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('kbd') || null;
}

export function initGlobalShortcut() {
  registerGlobalInitFunc('onGlobalShortcut', initShortcutKbd);

  // A <kbd> element next to an <input> declares a keyboard shortcut for that input.
  // When the matching key is pressed, the sibling input is focused.
  // When Escape is pressed inside such an input, the input is cleared and blurred.
  // The <kbd> element is shown/hidden automatically based on input focus and value.
  document.addEventListener('keydown', (e: KeyboardEvent) => {
    // Modifier keys are not supported yet
    if (e.ctrlKey || e.metaKey || e.altKey) return;

    const target = e.target as HTMLElement;

    // Handle Escape: clear and blur inputs that have an associated keyboard shortcut
    if (e.key === 'Escape') {
      const kbd = kbdFromElem(target);
      if (kbd) {
        (target as HTMLInputElement).value = '';
        (target as HTMLInputElement).blur();
      }
      return;
    }

    // Don't trigger shortcuts when typing in input fields or contenteditable areas
    if (target.matches('input, textarea, select') || target.isContentEditable) {
      return;
    }

    // Find kbd element with matching shortcut (case-insensitive), then focus its sibling input
    const key = e.key.toLowerCase();
    // At the moment, only a simple match. In the future, it can be extended to support modifiers and key combinations
    const kbd = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>(`.global-shortcut-wrapper > kbd[data-shortcut-keys="${CSS.escape(key)}"]`);
    if (!kbd) return;
    e.preventDefault();
    elemFromKbd(kbd)!.focus();

import {reactive} from 'vue';
import {GET} from '../modules/fetch.ts';
import {pathEscapeSegments} from '../utils/url.ts';
import {createElementFromHTML} from '../utils/dom.ts';
import {html} from '../utils/html.ts';

export type FileTreeItem = {
  entryName: string;
  entryMode: 'blob' | 'exec' | 'tree' | 'commit' | 'symlink' | 'unknown';
  entryIcon: string;
  entryIconOpen: string;
  fullPath: string;
  submoduleUrl?: string;
  children?: Array<FileTreeItem>;
};

export function createViewFileTreeStore(props: {repoLink: string, treePath: string, currentRefNameSubURL: string}) {
  const store = reactive({
    rootFiles: [] as Array<FileTreeItem>,
    selectedItem: props.treePath,

    async loadChildren(treePath: string, subPath: string = '') {
      // there is no git ref if no commits were made yet (an empty repo)
      if (!props.currentRefNameSubURL) return null;

      const response = await GET(`${props.repoLink}/tree-view/${props.currentRefNameSubURL}/${pathEscapeSegments(treePath)}?sub_path=${encodeURIComponent(subPath)}`);
      const json = await response.json();
      const poolSvgs = [];
      for (const [svgId, svgContent] of Object.entries(json.renderedIconPool ?? {})) {
        if (!document.querySelector(`.global-svg-icon-pool #${svgId}`)) poolSvgs.push(svgContent);
      }
      if (poolSvgs.length) {
        const svgContainer = createElementFromHTML(html`<div class="global-svg-icon-pool svg-icon-container"></div>`);
        svgContainer.innerHTML = poolSvgs.join('');
        document.body.append(svgContainer);
      }
      return json.fileTreeNodes ?? null;
    },

    async loadViewContent(url: string) {
      const u = new URL(url, window.origin);
      u.searchParams.set('only_content', 'true');
      const response = await GET(u.href);
      const elViewContent = document.querySelector('.repo-view-content')!;
      elViewContent.innerHTML = await response.text();
      const elViewContentData = elViewContent.querySelector('.repo-view-content-data');
      if (!elViewContentData) return; // if error occurs, there is no such element
      const t1 = elViewContentData.getAttribute('data-document-title');
      const t2 = elViewContentData.getAttribute('data-document-title-common');
      document.title = `${t1} - ${t2}`; // follow the format in head.tmpl: <head><title>...</title></head>
    },

    async navigateTreeView(treePath: string) {
      const url = store.buildTreePathWebUrl(treePath);
      window.history.pushState({treePath, url}, '', url);
      store.selectedItem = treePath;
      await store.loadViewContent(url);
    },

    buildTreePathWebUrl: (treePath: string) => `${props.repoLink}/src/${props.currentRefNameSubURL}/${pathEscapeSegments(treePath)}`,
  });
  return store;
}

    if (restoreFocus && focusInPopup) this.trigger.focus();
  }

  onPointerDownOutside = (e: Event) => {
    if (!this.contains(e.target as Node)) this.close(false);
  };

  // a native button fires "click" on Space keyup, which would toggle the menu shut again or double-activate an item
  preventSpaceClick = (e: KeyboardEvent) => {
    if (e.key === ' ') e.preventDefault();
  };

  onTriggerKeyDown = (e: KeyboardEvent) => {
    if (e.isComposing) return;
    if (e.key === 'Enter' || e.key === ' ' || e.key === 'ArrowDown') {
      this.open('first');
    } else if (e.key === 'ArrowUp') {
      this.open('last');
    } else {
      return;
    }
    e.preventDefault();
  };

  onPopupKeyDown = (e: KeyboardEvent) => {
    if (e.isComposing) return;
    const items = this.items();
    const current = items.indexOf(e.target as HTMLElement);
    if (e.key === 'Tab') {
      // focus the trigger and let the default action move on from there
      this.close(true);
      return;
    }
    if (e.key === 'Escape') {
      e.stopPropagation(); // don't also close a surrounding modal
      this.close(true);
    } else if (e.key === 'ArrowDown') {
      items[(current + 1) % items.length].focus();
    } else if (e.key === 'ArrowUp') {
      items.at(current <= 0 ? -1 : current - 1)!.focus();
    } else if (e.key === 'Home') {
      items[0].focus();
    } else if (e.key === 'End') {
      items.at(-1)!.focus();
    } else if (e.key === 'Enter' || e.key === ' ') {
      if (current < 0) return;
      items[current].click();
    } else if (e.key.length === 1 && !e.ctrlKey && !e.metaKey && !e.altKey) {
      this.focusByFirstChar(items, current, e.key);
    } else {
      return;
    }
    e.preventDefault();
  };

  focusByFirstChar(items: HTMLElement[], current: number, char: string) {
    const lower = char.toLowerCase();
    for (let i = 1; i <= items.length; i++) {
      const item = items[(current + i) % items.length];
      if (item.textContent.trim().toLowerCase().startsWith(lower)) {
        item.focus();
        return;
      }
    }
  }
